title: HTML Forms
subtitle: Make your webpage interactive and collect user data
description: Learn how to build contact forms, login forms, and feedback forms that turn your static portfolio into an interactive webpage. Forms are the gateway to backend - this is how your final app will collect messages from clients.

blocks.text: Your webpage looks good but can't talk back - let's fix that

So far your webpage from Lesson 1-5 is beautiful but static - people can see it but can't contact you, can't send you message, can't subscribe. Real webpages and apps need FORMS. Think of Jumia checkout, WhatsApp login, Google search bar - all forms. Today your portfolio becomes interactive and ready to collect client inquiries.
Open Menu > Practical now. You will build a contact form that will be part of your final complete webpage in Lesson 10. This form is what clients will use to hire you.
The form element - more than just inputs

form is a container that wraps all inputs. It has two critical attributes: action = where to send data (backend URL), method = how to send (GET for search/filter, POST for creating/sending data like contact messages). For now we will use action="#" meaning stay on same page, but in real app with Firebase or backend, action points to your server.

Inside form you need label for each input. Never create input without label - it's mandatory for accessibility. Screen readers read label to tell blind user what to type. Use for attribute on label that matches id on input to connect them programmatically.

blocks.title: Your first accessible form - structure
blocks.code:
<form action="#" method="POST">
 <label for="name">Your Name:</label>
 <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>
 
 <label for="email">Your Email:</label>
 <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
 
 <button type="submit">Send Message</button>
</form>
<!-- label for="name" connects to input id="name" -->
<!-- required means browser won't submit empty -->
blocks.output:
Your Name: [text box]
Your Email: [email box]
[Send Message button]

blocks.text: Input types - not just text, there are 20+ types

Beginners only use type="text" for everything. Professionals use correct type: email shows @ keyboard on mobile, tel shows number pad, number shows spinner, date shows calendar, password hides characters. Browser also validates automatically - email type checks if it contains @, url checks for https://.

blocks.text: Textarea, fieldset and legend - for professional forms

For long messages, don't use input type=text - use textarea which allows multiple lines, rows and cols. For grouping related inputs like Personal Info and Project Details, use fieldset with legend - it's semantic grouping that helps accessibility and visually groups with border. Real complete webpages use fieldset for sections.

blocks.text: Validation and attributes that make forms production-ready

Production forms need validation before sending to backend: required prevents empty submit, minlength/maxlength for text length, min/max for numbers, pattern for custom regex, placeholder gives hint but not label replacement. Also autocomplete helps users fill faster, and disabled vs readonly difference - disabled not sent to server, readonly sent but not editable.

blocks.title: Validation attributes - no JavaScript needed
blocks.code:
<form>
 <label for="username">Username (3-15 letters, required):</label>
 <input type="text" id="username" name="username" 
 required minlength="3" maxlength="15" 
 placeholder="PrinceDev" autocomplete="username">
 
 <label for="userage">Age (18-60 required):</label>
 <input type="number" id="userage" name="age" min="18" max="60" required>
 
 <label for="ghphone">Ghana Phone (pattern):</label>
 <input type="tel" id="ghphone" name="phone" 
 pattern="0[0-9]{9}" 
 placeholder="0240000000" 
 title="Enter 10 digits starting with 0">
 
 <label for="readonly">Account ID (readonly, sent to server):</label>
 <input type="text" id="readonly" value="USER123" readonly>
 
 <label for="disabled">Promo Code (disabled, not sent):</label>
 <input type="text" id="disabled" value="NEW2026" disabled>
</form>
blocks.output:
Username [3-15 chars required]
Age [18-60 required]
Ghana Phone [pattern 0 + 9 digits]
Account ID [readonly]
Promo [disabled]

blocks.title: Button types - submit, reset, button
blocks.code:
<form>
 <label for="search">Search my projects:</label>
 <input type="search" id="search" name="search" placeholder="Search...">
 <button type="submit">Search</button>
 
 <!-- Different button types -->
 <button type="submit">Send (submits form)</button>
 <button type="reset">Clear (resets all inputs)</button>
 <button type="button">Click Me (does nothing without JS, for JS actions)</button>
 
 <!-- Input type button vs button element -->
 <input type="submit" value="Submit via input">
 <input type="button" value="Button via input">
</form>
<!-- Always use <button> element - more flexible, can have HTML inside -->
blocks.output:
Search [search box with clear X]
[Send] [Clear] [Click Me]

blocks.question: You build contact form without label, using only placeholder="Your Name" inside input. It looks clean visually. Why will accessibility audit fail it critically?
options: It will pass because placeholder is modern replacement for label and screen readers read placeholder as label

It fails because placeholder disappears when user types, has low contrast, and many screen readers don't reliably announce placeholder as label; label with for/id association is mandatory for accessibility, placeholder is only hint not label
It fails because placeholder attribute is deprecated in HTML5 and must use title attribute instead of placeholder
It fails because placeholder only works for type=text not for email/tel, so email field needs label
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Placeholder ≠ label. This is WCAG failure - placeholder is hint, label is identity.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: What happens to placeholder when user starts typing? Can screen reader user know what field it is after typing?
blocks.reasoning: Placeholder disappears on input, low contrast, not reliably announced. Label is persistent, programmatically associated via for/id, required for accessibility.

blocks.question: You have radio buttons for service choice: Portfolio, Business, E-commerce. You gave each different name attribute: name="portfolio", name="business", name="ecommerce". User can select all three at once but should only select one. What is bug and fix?
options: Bug is using radio instead of checkbox - should use checkbox for single choice, radio is for multiple choices

Bug is that radio buttons with different name attributes are treated as separate groups, so all can be selected. Fix: Same name attribute for same group like name="service" for all three, different value attributes to distinguish
Bug is missing checked attribute - must add checked to all radios to make them single choice group
Bug is that radio requires fieldset wrapper - without fieldset radios allow multiple selection
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect debugging! Same name = same group, different name = different groups. This is core form logic.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: How does browser know which radios belong together? What groups them?
blocks.reasoning: Radio buttons are grouped by name attribute. Same name = one can be selected in group. Different names = separate groups, all can be selected.

blocks.question: You need form to send data to server to create new contact message. Should you use GET or POST and why? Also what happens if you use GET for contact form?
options: Use GET because GET is for sending data and POST is for getting data, so contact form should use GET to send message

Use POST because POST sends data in body not URL, more secure and no length limit, data not visible in URL history. GET appends data to URL visible in address bar, has length limit, should be used only for search/filter, not for creating/sending sensitive data
Both GET and POST are same, only difference is spelling, can use either for contact form with no impact
Use GET with action="POST" to combine benefits of both methods for contact forms
blocks.correctFeedback: Excellent backend awareness! Method choice matters for security, privacy and functionality.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Where does GET put data? Where does POST put data? Which is visible in URL?
blocks.reasoning: GET = data in URL query string, visible, limited length, for retrieval. POST = data in body, not visible in URL, no length limit, for creation/submission.

blocks.question: You have <input type="text" disabled value="GH₵500"> for price and <input type="text" readonly value="USER123"> for user ID in same form. Form submits. Which value reaches server and why difference matters?
options: Both values reach server because both disabled and readonly are sent, difference is only visual styling
Neither reaches server because both disabled and readonly prevent submission, need to use hidden type instead

Only readonly USER123 reaches server, disabled GH₵500 does NOT, because disabled inputs are excluded from form submission entirely, while readonly inputs are included but not editable - critical for pricing and IDs
Only disabled GH₵500 reaches server, readonly does not, because readonly means read-only display not for submission
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect form mastery! This distinction is crucial for e-commerce and user management.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Which attribute excludes from submission vs includes but prevents editing?
blocks.reasoning: disabled = not submitted, not focusable, excluded. readonly = submitted, focusable, not editable. Important for IDs (readonly) vs disabled promos.

blocks.question: You build login form with <input type="text" for password and <button>Login</button> without type. Users report password visible and pressing Enter in username field doesn't submit. What are two bugs?
options: Bug 1: Should be type="password" to mask characters, type="text" shows password visible. Bug 2: Button without type defaults to type="submit" actually so Enter should work, but if inside form with multiple buttons, first button might be submit; better to explicitly set type="submit" for main action and type="button" for others to control behavior
Bug 1: type="text" is correct for password, browser should mask automatically. Bug 2: Need type="login" for login button to enable Enter key
Bug 1: Need type="hidden" for password to hide. Bug 2: Need JavaScript to enable Enter key, HTML alone can't handle Enter
Bug 1: Password field must be <textarea> not input to hide. Bug 2: Button must be <input type="submit"> not <button>
blocks.correctFeedback: Excellent debugging! Password masking and button type defaults are critical for production login forms.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: What input type masks password? What does button default to when type omitted inside form?
blocks.reasoning: type=password masks, type=text shows. Button without type inside form defaults to submit, but explicit type is best practice to avoid ambiguity with multiple buttons.
